drills.q: What does a git blob object store?
drills.a: Only raw file content -- no filename, path, or permission bits. Those live in the tree object that references the blob.

drills.q: Physically, what is a git branch?
drills.a: A file holding a 40/64-hex commit SHA under .git/refs/heads/<name>. Moving a branch overwrites that file.

drills.q: Your teammate ran `git reset --hard` and lost three commits of unpushed work. What's your first command?
drills.a: git reflog -- find the SHA the branch pointed to before the reset, then git branch <name> <sha> to recreate a pointer to it.

drills.q: Why does rebase produce different commit hashes even when the resulting code is identical?
drills.a: A commit hash covers tree sha, parent sha(s), author/committer, and message. Rebase changes the parent field, changing the hash regardless of tree content.

drills.q: What specific race does `--force-with-lease` prevent that plain `--force` doesn't?
drills.a: It refuses to push if origin/<branch> as your local git last saw it doesn't match what's actually on the remote right now -- i.e. someone force- or regular-pushed since your last fetch. Plain --force overwrites blindly.

drills.q: A `git bisect run` script needs to report a commit that simply doesn't build. What exit code, and why not just call it bad?
drills.a: Exit 125 (skip). Calling an untestable commit 'bad' would corrupt the binary search by treating a build failure as evidence of the actual regression.

drills.q: Can the same branch be checked out in two different git worktrees at once? Why or why not?
drills.a: No -- all worktrees share one object database and one set of refs; two worktrees both holding that branch could each move the single ref independently with no reconciliation mechanism, so git refuses.

drills.q: You need to recover a commit, but git reflog on your machine shows nothing for it and it was never pushed anywhere. Is it recoverable?
drills.a: No -- the reflog is local-only and the object was never transmitted to any remote or other clone. This is the actual boundary of git's recoverability.

drills.q: A CI-automated git bisect converges on a commit inside a branch that was merged and fully reverted months ago. What's actually happening, mechanically?
drills.a: A revert commit undoes content but leaves the original commits fully present as ancestors in the DAG; bisect only evaluates the checked-out state at each commit and has no concept of 'later undone' -- it can land inside the reverted range if intermediate states reproduce the symptom differently.
